title: Our Students Decide How They'll Use AI in Our Class in the First 15 Minutes
author: Doan Winkel
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), September 7, 2026
summary: This piece lays out a specific, replicable fifteen-minute first-day classroom exercise designed to establish a course's AI norms through action rather than through the usual syllabus paragraph, which the author argues communicates only the instructor's anxiety rather than any actual standard. The method requires the teacher to generate a genuinely lazy, single-prompt AI answer to the semester's first real assignment beforehand, then have students grade that AI output in pairs against the actual rubric they'll be graded with, producing consistently low, 'competent but hollow' scores that students discover for themselves rather than being told. The pivotal move happens at minute eight, when the instructor asks what the AI answer would need to earn full credit -- forcing students to articulate the missing ingredients (specific evidence, a position, course-specific content) in their own words, which the author argues sticks harder than any instructor-stated policy because students said it publicly, to each other. The piece closes with an explicit caveat: the exercise should only be run on an assignment the teacher is confident about, since if the lazy AI answer scores well against the rubric, the exercise will publicly expose a design flaw in the assignment itself rather than in AI misuse.
points: The exercise deliberately replaces a stated AI policy with a demonstrated standard: students grade a real, admittedly-lazy AI answer against the actual course rubric, so the classroom's expectations become something they collectively discovered rather than something the syllabus merely asserted.

The minute-eight question ('what would this answer need to earn full credit?') is the exercise's real engine -- it makes students articulate the specific missing ingredients (evidence, position, course-specific content) in their own words, in front of peers, which the piece argues is more durable than any instructor-stated rule.

The author explicitly frames this as pre-empting misuse rather than punishing it after the fact: 'you never had to say don't cheat' because students concluded independently, from evidence, that the lazy version fails their own bar.

The built-in caution -- test the exercise privately first, and never run it live on an assignment you're unsure about -- acknowledges that the method doubles as a stress test of assignment design, since a lazy AI answer that scores well against the rubric exposes a problem with the task, not with AI.
quotes: Our students walked in with AI habits already installed. They didn't get them from us. They got them from a high school teacher who banned it, a professor last spring who pretended it didn't exist, and eight months of using it alone at midnight with nobody telling them whether they were doing it right.
A paragraph in a document tells students what you're afraid of. Fifteen minutes of doing something tells them what you expect.
You want the version a student would produce late the night before with no effort, because that's the version you're competing with all semester.

Listen for them naming what's missing without being coached: no specific evidence, no position, nothing from this course, nothing from their own head. They just described your standard better than your syllabus paragraph ever would.
You never had to say "don't cheat." They spent fifteen minutes finding out that the lazy version doesn't clear your bar.
If AI's lazy answer earns a B against your rubric, you found a bigger problem than a first-day exercise can fix, and doing this live will show thirty students that you found it.
